clue.text: Court hearing accepts main point upon reflection

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: a court hearing of a case is a trial

indicators.note: a reflection shows a thing mirrored, so the word for main point is read backwards

parts.note: the nub is the central point of a matter

explanation.surface: A court hearing grants the central argument after some thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court hearing' reads as one phrase, but 'Court' alone is the definition and 'hearing' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A tribunal is a body that sits in judgement on disputes, a kind of court.

clue.text: Clears up island engulfed by changing sea levels

indicators.note: something engulfed is swallowed up, so the island letter sits inside the other word

parts.note: tides are the rise and fall of sea level
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: Rising seas swamp an island and wash it clean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing' sounds like an anagram signal, but changing sea levels are simply tides.
explanation.definitionFit: To tidy is to clear up a mess, and tidies is the matching third-person form of the verb.

clue.text: Popular ballad that is about mother meeting her ruin

indicators.note: about means around here, so the two letters for 'that is' go round the rest

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, 'that is'
ma is an informal word for mother
gin is nicknamed mother's ruin in Britain

explanation.surface: A sentimental song about a mother who comes to grief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mother's ruin' is old British slang for gin, so 'her ruin', following mother, is gin.
explanation.definitionFit: Imagine is John Lennon's 1971 hit song, a slow and widely loved ballad.

clue.text: Gloomy detachment of soldiers encircles Lima

indicators.note: to encircle is to ring round, so the detachment word goes around the letter for Lima

parts.note: a unit is a detachment of troops
Lima is L in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A grim body of troops surrounds the Peruvian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Lima looks like the city in Peru; it is the radio code word for a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Unlit means without light, and a place without light is dark and gloomy.

clue.text: Camp originally established on River Wye, say, for sport

parts.note: camp and arch both mean affected or knowingly theatrical

indicators.note: originally points to how a word begins, so only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of established
R is the abbreviation for river

indicators.note: say asks for the spoken form, so the river's name stands for the letter it sounds like

parts.note: the River Wye's name is pronounced like the letter Y

explanation.surface: A camp beside the Welsh border River Wye, set up for sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River Wye' reads as one name, but River gives one letter and Wye another; the Wye flows between England and Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Archery, shooting arrows at a target with a bow, is a recognised sport.

clue.text: Key rings start to oxidise on the surface

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it, so the musical key goes around the other piece

parts.note: A flat is a musical key

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: first letter of oxidise

explanation.surface: A key ring begins to rust on its outer layer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key rings' looks like the things on a keychain; here 'Key' is a musical key and 'rings' means surrounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Something afloat floats on top of the water rather than sinking, so it is on the surface.

clue.text: Adult packed wrong pants

parts.note: packed means full

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the word before it is in a mess and its letters get reordered

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A grown-up put the wrong trousers in the suitcase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' looks like underwear or trousers in the surface; in British slang it means rubbish, a bad state.
explanation.definitionFit: Full-grown means having reached full size or maturity, which is what an adult has done.

clue.text: Old detective consumed son's drugs

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a PI is a private investigator
consumed food means ate
S is the abbreviation for son; the 's is read as 'has' and ignored

explanation.surface: A retired sleuth helped himself to his son's narcotics.
explanation.definitionFit: Opiates are drugs derived from opium, such as morphine and heroin.

clue.text: Model peruses gripping Spanish article about loom operators?

parts.note: the Model T was Ford's famous car

indicators.note: to grip is to hold tight, so the reading word holds the article within it

parts.note: to peruse is to read

indicators.note: about can mean turned around, so the Spanish article is read backwards

parts.note: el is the Spanish word for 'the'

explanation.surface: A fashion model studies a Spanish piece about weaving machines.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a definition by example: treadles work looms but also sewing machines and lathes.
explanation.definitionFit: A treadle is a foot pedal that drives a machine; on a hand loom treadles raise and lower the threads.

clue.text: Stand-off is not quick rugby player

parts.note: quick here means alive, as in 'the quick and the dead'
a lock is a second-row forward in rugby

explanation.surface: A stand-off half is not a fast rugby player, says the clue.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby a stand-off is a fly-half, which makes the surface about the sport; here it means an impasse. The old sense of 'quick' is living.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadlock is a situation where neither side can make progress, an impasse or stand-off.

clue.text: Spotted swimmer and reported location

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we want a word that sounds like the location word

parts.note: a location is a place

explanation.surface: Someone saw a swimmer and gave its whereabouts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' looks like a verb meaning seen; it describes the orange spots on the fish's skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaice is a flatfish with bright orange spots on its upper side, so a spotted swimmer.

clue.text: Ransack headquarters for Spooner's fastening device

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the first sounds of the pair are exchanged

parts.note: to ransack is to loot, and headquarters is a base; swap their opening sounds

explanation.surface: Raiders strip a command centre in search of something to tie things together.
explanation.definitionFit: A bootlace is a cord that ties a boot shut, a device for fastening it.

clue.text: Journalist essentially derided court's pronouncement

parts.note: ED, short for editor, is the usual crossword journalist

indicators.note: the essence of a word is at its core, so only its central letter is kept

parts.note: the middle letter of this seven-letter word
CT is an abbreviation for court; the 's is read as 'has' and ignored

explanation.surface: A reporter mocked a ruling from the bench.
explanation.definitionFit: An edict is an official order or proclamation issued by an authority, a formal pronouncement.

clue.text: Protracted contortion of leg and toe

indicators.note: a contortion is a twisting out of shape, so the letters that follow are bent into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A yoga pose that twists the leg and toe goes on and on.
explanation.definitionFit: Elongated means drawn out or lengthened, just as protracted means extended in time or length.

clue.text: Heartless German soldier pinches used, sleeveless jumper

indicators.note: to pinch is to grip between, so one piece holds the other inside it
without a heart means the central letter of the soldier's nickname is taken out

parts.note: Jerry is old British slang for a German soldier

indicators.note: sleeves are on the outside, so stripping them leaves only the inner letters

parts.note: the two inner letters of this word

explanation.surface: A cruel German soldier steals a worn, armless sweater.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is the British word for a sweater; Jersey is a knitted one named after the Channel Island.
explanation.definitionFit: A jersey is a knitted pullover, which in Britain is called a jumper.

clue.text: Rogue rats out deputy

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or wrong, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A crooked person exposes a corrupt second-in-command.
explanation.definitionFit: A surrogate is a substitute who stands in for another, which is what a deputy does.

clue.text: Excessively complex set containing one digit

parts.note: excessively means too much

indicators.note: to contain is to hold inside, so the jumbled word wraps around the next piece
something complex is tangled, so the letters of the following word are mixed up

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An overcomplicated collection holds a single number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digit' suggests a number, which fits the surface; here it is a toe.
explanation.definitionFit: Tootsie is a playful or childish word for a toe, and toes are digits of the foot.

clue.text: Tired-looking ship's company secures a mooring, periodically

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast within, so the crew word goes round the article

parts.note: a ship's company is its crew
taken as written

indicators.note: periodically means at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A weary sailor crew ties up at a berth now and then.
explanation.definitionFit: Careworn describes a face lined and tired from worry and strain, so tired-looking.

clue.text: Outrage surrounding soldier in dress

indicators.note: to surround is to enclose on all sides, so the outrage word goes around the soldier

parts.note: to outrage someone is to appal them
RE, the Royal Engineers, are British army soldiers

explanation.surface: People are outraged by a soldier wearing a frock.
explanation.definitionFit: Apparel is a formal word for clothing or garments, which is what dress means as a mass noun.

clue.text: Pictures friends crossing street on Ecstasy

indicators.note: something crossing a path cuts through it, so the street letters sit within the friends word

parts.note: pals are friends
ST is the abbreviation for street
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Photos of mates crossing the road while high.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means after: the drug letter comes below the street.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastels are pictures drawn in pastel crayons, a type of artwork.

clue.text: See 11
Expatriate from Northern India gatecrashing party

definitions.note: used as a verb, to send out of one's country

indicators.note: a gatecrasher pushes into an event uninvited, so these letters go inside the party word

parts.note: a bash is an informal word for a party
India is I in the NATO alphabet
N is the abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: An expat from the north of India turns up uninvited at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expatriate' reads as a noun, a person living abroad; it is the verb meaning to drive someone out of their country.
explanation.definitionFit: To banish someone is to send them into exile, which is what expatriating them as a verb means.

clue.text: Spotted things hidden by sailor beneath black undergarments

indicators.note: in a down clue what lies beneath comes lower, so the sailor piece is placed second, under the colour

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

indicators.note: a thing hidden by another is tucked inside it, so the sailor letters go around

parts.note: OS, ordinary seaman, is a sailor
dice are marked with spots

explanation.surface: Seamen were seen hiding garments under dark covers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beneath' places the black letter on top, since in a down clue what comes beneath is later.
explanation.definitionFit: A bodice is the close-fitting upper part of a dress, historically worn as an undergarment.

clue.text: Turn up records and incite ostentatious display

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up means reading from the bottom upwards, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: LPs are long-playing records
to incite is to urge

explanation.surface: Crank up the vinyl and whip the crowd into a showy frenzy.
explanation.definitionFit: A splurge is a lavish burst of spending or a showy display intended to impress.

clue.text: Tried fitting horse's heart in cooker

indicators.note: fitting something in is placing it inside, so that letter goes into the cooker

parts.note: a stove is a cooker

indicators.note: a heart is the centre, so only the middle letter of the animal is kept

parts.note: the middle letter of horse

explanation.surface: Someone attempted to fit a horse's heart into an oven.
explanation.definitionFit: Strove is the past tense of strive, to make great effort, so it means tried.

clue.text: Settled outcome, concealing last of arsenic in cake

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide within, so the outcome word wraps around everything else

parts.note: an end is a result or outcome
a scone is a small plain cake

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: final letter of arsenic

explanation.surface: A poisoner's case is resolved: arsenic was hidden in a cake.
explanation.walkthrough: The final letter of arsenic goes inside the cake, and that whole piece goes inside the outcome word; 'in cake' places the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ensconced means settled comfortably and securely in a place.

clue.text: Conspiracy involving international jet-setter?

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in, so the conspiracy word goes around the abbreviation

parts.note: a plot is a secret plan or conspiracy
I is the abbreviation for international

explanation.surface: A global plot hatched by a member of the wealthy travelling elite.
explanation.walkthrough: A jet-setter is normally a rich globetrotter; read literally, the question mark admits, it is one who sets a jet on its course.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot flies an aircraft and sets its direction, so playfully a setter of jets.

clue.text: Vessel carrying fashionable wine producer

indicators.note: a vessel carrying something holds it inside, so the pot wraps round the fashionable word

parts.note: a pot is a vessel
in means fashionable

explanation.surface: A ship transports a trendy vintner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wine producer' suggests a winemaker; the producer is a grape variety from which wine is made.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinot is a family of grape varieties, such as pinot noir, whose fruit produces wine.

clue.text: Some revolutionary tracts are popular works

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the run of letters reads backwards
some of the following words means only a run of their letters is used

parts.note: the run spans the end of tracts, all of are and the start of popular

explanation.surface: A few radical pamphlets have become bestsellers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'popular works' looks like a definition phrase, but popular supplies letters and only 'works' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Operas is the plural of opus, Latin for a work, as well as staged musical dramas, so works.

clue.text: Cranes regulated by satellite in hypothetical situation

indicators.note: regulating something puts it in a new order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
Io is a moon of Jupiter

explanation.surface: Cranes controlled from orbit, an imagined future case.
explanation.definitionFit: A scenario is a sketched-out sequence of events that might happen, a supposed or hypothetical situation.

clue.text: More inquisitive envoy's wife oddly ignored king

indicators.note: ignoring the odd-numbered positions leaves only the even ones in each word

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters
the second and fourth letters
R, for rex, is the king

explanation.surface: The ambassador's wife was strangely snubbed by the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters are taken from both envoy's and wife, so the apostrophe-s counts as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosier is the comparative of nosy, prying into others' business, so more inquisitive.

clue.text: Waiter's struggling with English, so to speak

indicators.note: a struggling worker is all over the place, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged, the 's included
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A foreign waiter battles with the English language, in a manner of speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: As it were is an idiom that flags a phrase as loosely worded, just as so to speak does.
